1:
The reign of a good king opens with the dry formula of accession, and the witnesses read it against its older twin in the book of Kings. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the notice stands word for word as 2 Kings 15:33, the chronicler altering nothing except to add the king's own name, Jotham, at the head. The reformed John Gill passes over the bare figures — five and twenty years old, sixteen years in Jerusalem — as matter already told, and sends the reader to the parallel record.

Over the naming of the mother the grammatical-historical eye lingers. Ellicott takes Jerushah the daughter of Zadok to be perhaps the daughter of that high priest Zadok named at 1 Chronicles 6:12, comparing the like notice of a queen-mother's descent at 2 Chronicles 22:11. If so, the good king was born of a union between the house of David and the house of the priesthood, a pairing that may help to account for the reverence for the temple his reign would show — a reverence the very next verse will single out for praise.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the whole arc of the reign in a breath, as a table of contents to what follows: Jotham succeeds his father Uzziah and reigns well; he raises his buildings; he wages his successful wars; and the chapter closes with the general account of his acts, his reign, and his death. It is, on Clarke's reading, a reign almost wholly favourable — the rare notice of a king of Judah against whom the sacred writer records no personal apostasy at all.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill defers to the older annals; Ellicott secures the borrowed wording and traces the queen-mother to the priestly line; Clarke sketches the shape of the reign the verse introduces. Between them they set Jotham before the reader as the son and heir of Uzziah, inheriting a kingdom left strong and prosperous, and, unlike his father at the last, keeping his hands clean of the one great sin that had brought that father low. The sixteen years in Jerusalem summed up here would prove, on Clarke's reckoning, the last long stretch of settled strength the southern kingdom would know before the storms that the reign of his son was about to loose upon it — so that the bare regnal notice, read forward, is already the quiet high-water mark of Judah's peace.
2:
That Jotham did what was right, yet with two reservations attached, gives the witnesses their whole matter here. The reformed John Gill notes only that he did that which was right, as the parallel had already said. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as measuring the king by his father: he did right according to all that Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD — the one qualification being that he did not repeat his father's presumption. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the point: Jotham copied his father's conduct so far as it was constitutional, and avoided his transgression, the sacrilege for which Uzziah had been struck with leprosy when he thrust himself into the priest's office at 2 Chronicles 26:16.

Ellicott, of the same grammatical-historical school, explains why the clause is here at all. The chronicler adds this reservation upon his general commendation because he alone had recorded Uzziah's sacrilege; the author of Kings, having said nothing of it, had no need of the exception. And the closing words, and the people did yet corruptly, Ellicott takes as a paraphrase of what stands at 2 Kings 15:35 — that the people still sacrificed and burnt incense on the high places — adding that the prophets of those very days, at Micah 3:10-12 and Hosea 4:1-2, bear witness to a deep-seated moral corruption sapping the nation's strength.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the lesson of the qualified praise: Jotham did according to all that his father did, except in his miscarriages; and we must not imitate even those we most esteem any further than they do well, but let their failings be warnings to us to walk the more circumspectly. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns to the people's fault, and half-turns it back upon the king. The people still did corruptly; and perhaps, Henry allows, Jotham was wanting toward the reformation of the land, for men may be very good and yet not have the courage and zeal to do all they might. Yet the words certainly cast blame upon the people themselves, who under so good a king would still not be good.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the fact; Keil and Clarke read the temple-reservation as the mark of a son wiser than his father; Ellicott sets both clauses against their sources and hears the prophets behind them; Wesley draws the caution against imitating the great in their faults; Henry weighs where the blame for the people's corruption should fall. Between them they show a king genuinely upright, careful not to overstep as his father had, reigning over a people whose hearts he could not, or did not, fully turn.
3:
The one building of Jotham's that the older history also records draws the witnesses to the temple gate and the city wall. The reformed John Gill marks simply that he built the high gate in the house of the LORD. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun — he it was that built — and explains that to build here means to restore and beautify, the same statement standing at 2 Kings 15:35. The high gate he would rather call the upper gate, the northern gate of the inner or upper court at Ezekiel 9:2; and since the north was reckoned the holy quarter, at Isaiah 14:13 and Psalms 48:2, the north gate would be the principal entrance.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch agrees that this upper gate of the house of Jahve was the only work of the reign mentioned in the book of Kings, and adds that Jotham did not stop there but continued the fortifying of Jerusalem his father had begun, building much at the wall of the Ophel — the southern slope of the temple mountain, whose wall connected Zion with the temple hill, and at which Uzziah had already laboured at 2 Chronicles 26:9. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following the Targum, takes Ophel for the wall of the interior palace, some part of the wall of Jerusalem that was most pregnable, and therefore fortified by Jotham in a particular manner.

Ellicott gathers the smaller notes. The wall of Ophel he too sets on the southern slope, the line of works securing the city against attack from the south and east; neither this detail nor the next three verses, he observes, are found in the parallel account, and the style and contents of the passage indicate a good ancient source behind the chronicler's hand. The very word much, larob, he marks as one of the chronicler's favourite terms. And the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the same qualification the grammatical-historical witnesses had made: the king built in the sense of repairing, for the gate stood before his day.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the gate; Ellicott and Keil identify the upper northern gate and the Ophel wall and trace both to a good source; Clarke supplies the Targum's reading of the pregnable wall; Wesley secures the sense of built. Between them they show Jotham as a builder in his father's line — beautifying the LORD's house at its chief gate and strengthening the city's weakest flank — the works of a reign that spent its peace not in luxury but in the sober labour of fortification, and that honoured the temple its king was careful never to profane.
4:
From the city Jotham's building turns to the countryside, and the witnesses follow him into the hills and woods. The reformed John Gill sets the scene plainly: he built cities in the mountainous part of the land, the hill country of Judea. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the continuation of Uzziah's programme: Jotham built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests built castles and towers, carrying on his father's works for the protection of the herds recorded at 2 Chronicles 26:10. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the towers their purpose: these castles and towers he built for the protection of the country people against marauders.

Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, brings the philologist's precision. Literally, he says, the verse runs and cities built he in the hill region of Judah, again comparing his father's like labours at 2 Chronicles 26:10; the word for castles, biraniyoth, is the same term he had explained at 2 Chronicles 17:12. But Ellicott will not let the reader admire the fortresses uncritically, for the contemporary prophets denounced the popular confidence in fenced cities as a kind of treason against Jehovah, who was himself the shield and fortress of his people at Psalms 18:1 and Isaiah 12:2. "Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth palaces; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities," ran the word of Hosea 8:14, to which he adds the like reproofs at Isaiah 2:15 and Isaiah 17:3-4.

So even in recording a good king's prudence the grammatical-historical witness hears a warning note. The cities and towers were wise defence, a shepherd-king's care for his flocks and his frontier folk; yet the prophets of the age were already teaching that walls are no security when the Maker who is the true fortress has been forgotten. Jotham, the witnesses imply, did not fall into that error — his strength, the next verses will say, rested on his walking before God — but the building itself carried a lesson his son would fail to learn.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the cities in the hill country; Keil and Ellicott bind the work to Uzziah's and fix the term for the castles; Clarke names their use against raiders; Ellicott alone sounds the prophetic caution against trusting in them. Between them they show a reign quietly consolidating its land, fortifying the highlands, watching the woods, and guarding the herds — the peaceable industry of a king making his kingdom strong against the day of trouble.
5:
The single military campaign of the reign now comes into view, and the witnesses weigh both the victory and the tribute that followed. The reformed John Gill recalls the long history behind it: the Ammonites had been brought into subjection by David, but in later times endeavoured to cast off the yoke, and even invaded Judah in the days of Jehoshaphat; now under Jotham they resisted again, but did not succeed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill in the sequence: the Ammonites had paid tribute to Uzziah, and after his death would seem to have refused it, so that Jotham made them tributary again by force of arms, compelling them after their defeat to render a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cor of wheat, and as much barley, and to bring him the same amount in the second year and the third — after which, the three years past, they again fell away.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, adds the measure and the geography. He reads the opening as he also, like his father, fought with the king of the sons of Ammon; the ten thousand measures are korim, the kor perhaps equal to our quarter, as at 1 Kings 4:22 and 2 Chronicles 2:10, and the land of Ammon is fertile of grain to this day. The closing clause he renders, this tribute did the children of Ammon restore to him, and in the second year and the third — the payments ceasing after three years, perhaps because Ammon took advantage of the outbreak of the Syro-Ephraite war that fell towards the end of the reign at 2 Kings 15:37.

Over the exact relation of victory to tribute the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke raises a doubt. That Jotham brought Ammon under a heavy tribute for three years is plain; but whether this was simply the effect of his prevailing against them is, he thinks, not so evident. Some, he reports, hold rather that Ammon paid the tribute for three years and then revolted, and that Jotham's attack and their utter subjection followed as the consequence — the order of conquest and payment reversed.

So the witnesses agree on the facts and differ only over their sequence. Gill sets the revolt in its Davidic frame; Keil and Ellicott read a victory first and tribute after, lapsing at three years as the Syrian war drew on; Clarke leaves open whether the subjugation preceded or followed the tribute. Between them they show the one war of a peaceful reign — a decisive stroke against an old vassal, rich payment in silver and grain, and, at the last, the same restlessness on the frontier that every reign of Judah had to meet.
6:
The chronicler pauses to render his verdict, and the witnesses gather at his favourite theme — that strength follows faithfulness. The reformed John Gill reads the cause plainly from the acts just told: Jotham became mighty, having built his towers and castles, fortified his cities, and conquered his enemies. But the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press past the outward works to the inward ground the verse assigns: Jotham strengthened himself in the kingdom, attaining greater power because he made his ways firm before Jahve — walked steadfastly before him, and did not incur guilt by falling away into idolatry or by any faithless infringement of the LORD's rights, as his father Uzziah had done in usurping the office of the priests at 2 Chronicles 26:16.

Keil hears in the phrase all his wars, at the following verse, a hint that Jotham waged other successful campaigns than the Ammonite one; and he weighs, only to doubt, the older commentators' guess that the war with Rezin and Pekah — which the LORD, at 2 Kings 15:37, began in his days to send against Judah — should be reckoned among them; for the placing of that notice at the very end of the Kings account suggests the war broke out only toward the close of the reign, too late for Jotham to undertake much against it.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, dwells on the wording as a moral reflection of the writer upon the preceding facts. Became mighty is the chronicler's customary phrase, strengthened himself, as at 2 Chronicles 13:21; prepared his ways means directed or established them, at Proverbs 21:29 and comparably at 2 Chronicles 12:14 and 2 Chronicles 20:33. Jotham directed his ways before, that is toward, Jehovah his God, as at 1 Chronicles 12:17 and 1 Samuel 7:3; or perhaps before means simply as in the sight of God, in the manner of the walk before me commanded at Genesis 17:1.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the practical rule the verse teaches: Jotham prospered and became mighty, and the more steadfast we are in religion, the more mighty we are, both to resist evil and to do good. The witnesses do not divide. Gill counts the works; Keil and Ellicott fix the phrase and its theology, and Keil the wars behind it; Henry turns it to a maxim. Between them they name the secret of the reign — a king strong because his ways were set, steadily and in God's sight, toward the God who was the true fortress of his people.
7:
The reign begins to be wound up with the customary formula of reference, and the witnesses attend to what the formula quietly conceals. The reformed John Gill reads the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars, as pointing beyond the Ammonite campaign to his wars with the Syrians and the ten tribes as well. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the observation: where the parallel at 2 Kings 15:36 reads only and all that he did, the chronicler has varied the phrase to and all his wars and his ways, seemingly in order to hint at the Syro-Ephraite war named at 2 Kings 15:37.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke expands the hint into history. It was in Jotham's days, according to 2 Kings 15:37, that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel began to cut Judah short — the first pressure of the confederacy that would come to a head under his son. Clarke notes too the poverty of the record: there is not so much preserved in the books of Kings as we have here in the Chronicles, and in both places only abridged accounts survive, the larger histories to which the formula points having long been lost. And he pronounces the reign's place in the story of the nation: the reign of Jotham was properly the last politically prosperous reign among the Jews; Hezekiah and Josiah would afterward do much to preserve the divine worship, but Judah continued to be cut short until at last it was wholly ruined.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading the same verse, hear in all his wars the sign that Jotham's military record was fuller than the two brief campaigns Scripture stops to name, and set the whole notice as the frame within which the death-formula of the next verses will fall. The witnesses do not divide. Gill reads the wars widely; Ellicott marks the chronicler's deliberate variation of the Kings phrase; Clarke unfolds the Syrian pressure it hints at, laments the lost fuller histories, and fixes the reign as the last prosperous one; Keil confirms the hint of other wars.

Between them they show the sacred writer closing an account he knows to be partial — referring the reader to records now perished, and letting a single altered phrase carry the weight of a gathering danger. Jotham's sixteen years had been full and strong; but the formula that ends them already looks toward the shadow, for the sword of Syria and Ephraim was even then being drawn, and the prosperity summed up in this verse was the last the kingdom would enjoy before its long decline.
8:
The regnal figures already given at the head of the chapter now return, and the witnesses make the repetition itself their subject. The reformed John Gill notes only that the same is here repeated as was said before — the king five and twenty years old at his accession, sixteen years upon the throne. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the doubled notice as a word-for-word repetition of 2 Kings 15:33, save that it omits the last clause about the queen-mother already given in the opening verse; and he offers the source-critical explanation that in one of the chronicler's authorities this notice may have stood at the beginning of the reign, and in another at the end, which would account for its appearing twice.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch reaches the very same conclusion by the same road: the repetition of the chronological statement already made is probably to be explained by supposing that two authorities were used, each of which contained the remark, the compiler taking it over from both. It is, for these witnesses, a small window onto the chronicler's method — the seam where two sources have been stitched together showing plainly on the surface of the text, an accession-formula standing once where the reign opens and once where it closes.

That seam repays notice, for it belongs to the same pattern the witnesses have traced through the whole chapter: the chronicler taking over the older annals almost verbatim where they served him, as in the borrowed notice of 2 Kings 15:33, while drawing on further authorities for the buildings and wars that Kings never mentions. The very awkwardness of the doubled figures is thus a mark of fidelity rather than carelessness: the compiler has preserved what each of his sources gave him, even at the cost of saying the same thing twice.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill registers the repetition; Ellicott and Keil, with one voice, account for it by the meeting of two sources and note the clause about the queen-mother dropped the second time. Between them they let a bare and seemingly redundant verse testify to the way the sacred history was composed — not spun from a single hand, but gathered faithfully out of older records, whose joins the honest compiler did not trouble to hide. The figures that open and close the reign are the same because the two authorities behind the chronicler agreed, and he would not silence either.
9:
The reign closes as quietly as it ran — Jotham slept with his fathers, was buried in the city of David, and Ahaz his son reigned in his stead — and the witnesses read the honourable ending against the storm they know is coming. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the plain sense: the king died as his fathers died, was laid among them in the city of David with no note of dishonour, and passed the throne to his son. There is here none of the withheld burial or the loveless funeral that the sacred writer reserves for the apostate kings; Jotham goes to his grave with the customary honours of the house of David.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the death at the hinge of the nation's history. The reign of Jotham, he says, was properly the last politically prosperous reign among the Jews; after him Hezekiah and Josiah would still do much to preserve the divine worship, but the kingdom itself continued to be cut short until at last it was wholly ruined. The good king's death is thus the close of an age — the last long stretch of settled strength before the descent begins.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws from the same succession its sober providential lesson. The LORD, he observes, often removes wise and pious rulers, and sends others in their room whose follies and vices punish a people that valued not their mercies. It is precisely what the next chapter will show: a people who under a good king still did corruptly are now given over to a king who will lead them into open apostasy, and the removal of Jotham becomes itself a judgment upon those who had not prized him.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil fixes the death, the honoured burial, and the succession; Clarke marks the reign as the last prosperous one and the turn toward ruin; Henry hears in the changing of the guard the hand of a God who takes away the good ruler an unthankful people had undervalued. Between them they close the account of Jotham on a double note, of honour and of foreboding. The king is buried with his fathers, mourned and esteemed; yet the name of the son who reigns in his stead, Ahaz, hangs over the verse like a cloud, for the reader who knows what follows understands that the peace summed up in these nine verses is about to be spent, and the kingdom that Jotham left strong is about to be led, by the child of his own house, down into the long night of its undoing.
